target_customer: Low-income Americans seeking Chapter 7 bankruptcy; paid for by philanthropies, legal aid funds, government grants and voluntary tips rather than users
problem: Low-income people cannot afford a lawyer or fees for bankruptcy, so they stay in debt even when bankruptcy would help.
business_model: 501(c)(3) nonprofit offering a free guided filing tool, funded by philanthropy and legal aid grants, with a pay what you think is fair tip model
product_category: Legal tech nonprofit, consumer debt relief

founders.name: Rohan Pavuluri
prior_employers: Harvard Law School Access to Justice Lab (research assistant)
founders.background_notes: Sources: Harvard Magazine, Stanford Law startup snapshot 2016-10-03, TechCrunch 2019-01-16.

founders.name: Jonathan Petts
founders.background_notes: Bankruptcy attorney who did pro bono work; the only founder listed on the YC page. Sources: Harvard Magazine, technical.ly 2017-05-30.

technical_complexity.rationale: Generating correct Chapter 7 forms across many courts and exemption rules needs legal logic encoded in software, but it is a form workflow rather than novel technology.

defensibility.rationale: Philanthropic funding, legal aid relationships and accumulated case data are hard to copy, but unauthorized practice of law rules also limit Upsolve itself.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: TechCrunch 2019 noted most lawyers did not want these cases; no incumbent copied the free model. The main later threat was legal challenge, such as a Maryland court finding on its Exemption Editor.

market_need_then: Upsolve reported about $16 million in bankruptcies for 400 people and debt diagnosis for 5,000 users in 2018 (TechCrunch 2019-01-16). Chapter 7 court fees were about $340 and lawyers averaged $1,450 (technical.ly 2017-05-30).

branding.domain_note: Uses upsolve.org (nonprofit domain); acquisition history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Plain, reassuring and careful to state it is not a lawyer.

branding.brand_signature: The 'TurboTax for bankruptcy' framing and debt-erased counters on its site
branding.community_and_virality: Press such as the NYT Good Tech Award, ABA Legal Rebels profile and Chronicle of Philanthropy podcast; no merch found.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong cause press and trust positioning in access to justice circles, but a niche brand with limited consumer reach beyond its audience.

outcome_analysis: Upsolve, a nonprofit YC company, built a free Chapter 7 tool funded by Legal Services Corporation, Robin Hood, Schmidt Futures and others, and by its own count has helped 29,000 people erase about $1.3 billion of debt. It stays active with a small team; the main risk is legal, with a Second Circuit loss in September 2025 on its volunteer debt advice program and a Maryland ruling on one software feature.
notes: As a nonprofit, funding is grants and philanthropy; amounts are mostly undisclosed. Wikipedia and Business Today list Y Combinator, Legal Services Corporation, Robin Hood, Harvard and Eric Schmidt (Business Today says $3M+); FundedIQ shows $4.2M in 2024-09; none verified so not recorded. Wikipedia adds Mark Hansen as a third founder, not confirmed by an opened primary source. Grant dates in 2017 are the article date, not stated dates. Competitors: Stanford 2016 and technical.ly 2017 and TechCrunch 2019 name none (competition was stigma against bankruptcy), so the list is empty. Outcome search found litigation (2022 suit, Sept 2025 Second Circuit loss) but no shutdown or acquisition. Name origin is discussed in a 2020 Business Today podcast that was not read.
